Neurology · published research

Binswanger's disease

One non-randomized report described improved cerebral circulation and clinical measures after invasive transcatheter PBM, but Binswanger-specific results were not consistently separated from those for vascular parkinsonism.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

One non-randomized report described improved cerebral circulation and clinical measures after invasive transcatheter PBM, but Binswanger-specific results were not consistently separated from those for vascular parkinsonism.

Summary of the Evidence

One full clinical publication is classified specifically under Binswanger’s disease. It is a non-randomized controlled report involving 27 people with Binswanger’s disease alongside 62 people with vascular parkinsonism. A 2021 Alzheimer-related conference poster describes 17 Binswanger cases treated by the same author using the same invasive method. The poster may overlap with the earlier clinical series, but the relationship is not confirmed; it is not counted as an independent cohort (Maksimovich et al. 2019 Maksimovich et al. 2021).

Human and clinical evidence

The 2019 report compared 14 treated and 13 conservatively treated participants with Binswanger’s disease. The paper describes changes in cerebral microcirculation, cognition, and clinical status after treatment, but several headline outcome percentages are pooled across the Binswanger and vascular-parkinsonism groups. They should not be read as a Binswanger-only response rate. The study did not randomly allocate participants, and the abstract does not provide a blinded, independently assessed disease-specific treatment effect.

Animal evidence

No animal study is listed in the exact Binswanger category.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No standalone cell or ex-vivo study is listed for this indication.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The reported technique is invasive intracerebral transcatheter PBM, rather than light applied through the scalp. The database record gives 633 nm red visible light, laser power of 25–45 mW, total energy of 29–106 J, and exposure times of 20–40 minutes, usually as one procedure. The paper does not establish how these parameters compare with noninvasive transcranial devices. The results therefore apply only to this specialized catheter procedure and cannot be used to infer the effect of ordinary external PBM.

Interpretation

The clinical report describes improvement after transcatheter treatment, including circulation and cognition measures. This is a favorable reported direction in a small Binswanger subgroup, but the design and pooled reporting leave substantial uncertainty about the size of a disease-specific effect. Replication with randomized allocation, separate Binswanger results, and transparent procedural safety reporting would provide a clearer test.

Evidence strength in source summaryVery low for clinical outcomes after invasive transcatheter PBM
Publications and records1 full direct clinical publication

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

The direct clinical report included 27 people with Binswanger’s disease in a non-randomized comparison and combined some outcome reporting with a larger vascular-parkinsonism group. A later conference abstract includes 17 Binswanger cases from the same author and technique, with overlap likely but unconfirmed. Independent controlled studies reporting disease-specific outcomes and procedural safety would be needed to strengthen this evidence.

  • No animal or in-vitro study identified.
